subject: Chemistry

outcomes.text: Explain how an element’s mass spectrum relates quantitatively to its isotope masses.
Use a single-element mass spectrum to identify isotopes and determine their natural relative abundances.
Estimate an element’s average atomic mass by weighting isotope masses according to their relative abundances.
Use dimensional analysis and moles to calculate substance amounts or relative particle numbers.
Relate measurable sample mass to the number of particles participating in chemical changes.
Use Avogadro’s number to convert between moles and constituent particles or formula units.
Connect atomic or molecular mass in amu with molar mass and sample particle count.
Relate a pure substance’s mass composition of elements to its empirical formula.
Distinguish molecular substances from substances consisting of atoms or ions in fixed formula-unit proportions.
Apply definite proportions: a compound always contains its elements in the same mass ratio.
Identify an empirical formula as the smallest whole-number elemental ratio in a compound.
Relate elemental mass composition to the composition of substances in a mixture.
Distinguish pure substances from mixtures based on the types and variable proportions of particles present.
Use elemental analysis to determine atomic ratios and assess a substance’s purity.
Represent ground-state electron configurations of atoms and ions using the Aufbau principle.
Describe atoms as electrons surrounding a nucleus containing protons and neutrons.
Use Coulomb’s law to determine how charged particles’ separation and charges affect their force.
Describe shells, subshells, core electrons, and valence electrons through ground-state configurations and the periodic table.
Explain ionization-energy differences using electron–nucleus distance, shielding, and effective nuclear charge.
Relate PES spectra to ground-state configurations and electron–nucleus interactions.
Interpret PES peak positions as subshell electron energies and peak heights as electron counts.
Explain periodic atomic-property trends using electronic structure and periodicity.
Explain periodic-table organization through recurring properties, electron configurations, and shell or subshell filling.
Predict ionization energy, atomic and ionic radii, electron affinity, and electronegativity trends.
Use periodicity to estimate atomic-property values when direct data are unavailable.
Relate elemental reactivity trends to valence electrons and periodicity.
Explain bond formation likelihood through interactions between valence electrons and atomic nuclei.
Predict that elements in the same periodic-table column tend to form analogous compounds.
Predict typical ionic charges from valence-electron counts and periodic-table positions.
Relate bonding type to the properties of the elements forming the bond.
Describe periodic electronegativity trends using atomic structure, shell models, and Coulomb’s law.
Identify shared valence electrons between similarly electronegative atoms as a nonpolar covalent bond.
Explain polar covalent bonds, including partial charges, bond dipoles, and their continuum with ionic bonding.
Use electronegativity and compound properties to distinguish generally ionic bonds from covalent bonds.
Describe metallic solids as having valence electrons delocalized among the metal atoms.
Represent how atomic distance and other factors affect interaction strength and potential energy.
Interpret potential-energy-versus-distance graphs to identify equilibrium bond length and bond energy.
Relate covalent bond length to atomic core size and bond order; higher-order bonds are shorter and stronger.
Use Coulomb’s law to relate ionic interaction strength to ion charges and separation.
Model ionic solids consistently with Coulomb’s law and the properties of their ions.
Describe ionic crystals as periodic three-dimensional arrays maximizing attraction and minimizing repulsion.
Model metallic solids and alloys to show their structures and interactions.
Represent metallic bonding as positive ions surrounded by delocalized valence electrons.
Explain interstitial alloys as smaller atoms occupying spaces among larger atoms.
Explain substitutional alloys as similar-sized atoms replacing one another in a lattice.
Represent molecules using Lewis diagrams.
Construct Lewis diagrams using established principles.
Use resonance and formal charge in Lewis diagrams to model molecular structures and properties.
Include resonance when equivalent Lewis structures are possible to improve molecular predictions.
Use octet compliance and formal charge to select the best among valid Lewis structures.
Recognize limitations of Lewis structures, especially for species with odd numbers of valence electrons.
Use Lewis structures, VSEPR, bond order, and polarity to explain molecular structural and electron properties.
Use electron-pair repulsion to predict electron arrangements around a central atom.
Use Lewis structures and VSEPR to predict molecular geometry, angles, bond properties, dipoles, and hybridization.
Relate sp, sp2, and sp3 hybridization to electron arrangements and ideal bond angles.
Explain sigma and pi bonding from orbital overlap, including effects on bond strength and rotation.

units.title: Unit 3: Properties of Substances and Mixtures

outcomes.text: Relate molecular structure to intermolecular-force strength for identical or different chemical species.
Explain London dispersion forces as attractions between temporary dipoles, often dominant in large molecules.
Explain how polar molecules’ dipole moments create additional interactions with other chemical species.
Use partial-charge signs and orientations to compare dipole-dipole and ion-dipole interaction strengths.
Identify hydrogen bonding as attraction involving hydrogen bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine.
Recognize that large biomolecules can have noncovalent interactions within or between molecules.
Relate macroscopic properties to a substance’s particulate structure and particle interactions.
Relate intermolecular-force strength to vapor pressure, boiling point, and melting point.
Use particulate representations to show how intermolecular interactions produce macroscopic properties.
Relate ionic-solid structure and interactions to brittleness, phase-change temperatures, vapor pressure, and conductivity.
Relate covalent-network structures and bonding to hardness, rigidity, and high melting points.
Relate molecular-solid structure and weak intermolecular forces to low melting points and lack of conductivity.
Relate metallic bonding and alloy structure to conductivity, malleability, ductility, and rigidity.
Explain how noncovalent interactions affect the shape and properties of biomolecules and polymers.
Represent solid, liquid, and gas phases with particulate-level models.
Distinguish crystalline and amorphous solids by particle arrangement and limited particle motion.
Describe liquid particles as closely packed, mobile, colliding, and influenced by interparticle forces.
Explain why solids and liquids of one substance usually have similar molar volumes.
Relate gas-particle motion and spacing to temperature, pressure, volume, and absence of fixed shape or volume.
Use the ideal gas law to relate macroscopic properties of gas samples or mixtures.
Apply PV = nRT to connect pressure, volume, amount, and temperature.
Relate partial pressures to mole fractions and calculate total pressure by summing component pressures.
Use graphs to describe relationships among gas pressure, volume, temperature, and amount.
Relate particle motion to gas properties using kinetic theory, particulate models, and graphs.
Use kinetic molecular theory and Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions to connect particle motion with gas properties.
Describe continuous random particle motion and relate kinetic energy to mass and velocity.
Relate Kelvin temperature to particles’ average kinetic energy.
Interpret Maxwell-Boltzmann graphs showing particle energy or velocity distributions at a temperature.
Explain nonideal gas behavior using interparticle attractions and particle volumes.
Explain deviations from ideal behavior through molecular attractions near condensation and finite particle volumes at high pressure.
Calculate solute-particle amount, solution volume, or molarity.
Distinguish homogeneous solutions from heterogeneous mixtures using whether macroscopic properties vary throughout the sample.
Express solution composition in different ways, especially using molarity as solute amount per liter of solution.
Use particulate models to show component interactions and relative concentrations in mixtures.
Use solution models to depict component concentrations and interactions among dissolved particles.
Explain separation results by relating them to differences in intermolecular interactions.
Explain how chromatography separates solution components through differing intermolecular attractions and reveals their relative polarities.
Relate ionic and molecular compound solubility in aqueous or nonaqueous solvents to intermolecular interactions.
Predict that substances with similar intermolecular interactions are more likely to dissolve in or mix with each other.
Connect electromagnetic-spectrum regions with the molecular motions or electronic transitions they produce.
Identify microwave, infrared, and ultraviolet/visible radiation with rotational, vibrational, and electronic transitions, respectively.
Explain how absorbing or emitting photons changes an atom’s or molecule’s energy during electronic transitions.
Relate photon absorption or emission to an equal increase or decrease in the species’ energy.
Use c = λν and E = hν to relate wavelength, frequency, light speed, and photon energy.
Relate solution absorbance to concentration, path length, and molar absorptivity.
Use A = εbc to relate absorbance to molar absorptivity, path length, and concentration.
When wavelength and path length are fixed, relate absorbance directly to absorbing-particle concentration and maximum-wavelength measurement sensitivity.
Distinguish physical changes from chemical changes using evidence about matter’s properties and composition.
Physical changes alter properties or phases without changing composition; forming or separating mixtures are common examples.
Chemical changes create new substances; heat, light, gas, precipitate, or color change may indicate them.
Write balanced molecular or net ionic equations for physical changes, specified substances, and participating ions.
Represent every physical and chemical process with a balanced equation.
Chemical equations show atoms rearranging while conserving each element’s atoms and total charge.
Use molecular, complete ionic, or net ionic forms according to the reaction’s context.
Create a consistent particulate model for a chemical reaction or physical process.
Translate balanced chemical equations into symbolic representations of particles.
Relate observable properties to bond interactions in chemical and physical processes.
Bond breaking or formation generally indicates chemical change, whereas changing intermolecular interactions generally indicates physical change.
Some physical processes, such as dissolving salts, can also break chemical bonds.
Use balanced equations to explain changes in reactant and product quantities.
Calculate product quantities from reactants or reactant quantities from products using atom conservation.
Use equation coefficients as mole ratios in quantitative chemical calculations.
Combine stoichiometry with the ideal gas law and molarity calculations for gases and solutions.
Determine a titration’s equivalence point from titrant and analyte amounts when the reaction is complete.
Use a known, specific titrant reaction to determine analyte amount; recognize endpoint indicators of equivalence.
Classify reactions as acid-base, oxidation-reduction, or precipitation.
Acid-base reactions transfer one or more protons between chemical species.
Redox reactions transfer electrons, changing oxidation numbers; combustion reacts a substance with oxygen.
In redox reactions, electrons move from the oxidized species to the reduced species.
Assign oxidation numbers to identify which species undergo oxidation and reduction.
Precipitation mixes aqueous ions to form a sparingly soluble ionic compound; sodium, potassium, ammonium, and nitrate salts dissolve.
Identify Brønsted-Lowry acids, bases, and conjugate pairs from proton-transfer reactions.
A Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton, while a base accepts one.
In water, water molecules can accept or donate protons during acid-base reactions.
Identify conjugate acid-base pairs and compare their relative strengths when species ionize in water.
Represent balanced redox equations using half-reactions.
Construct balanced redox equations by combining appropriate half-reactions.
Explain how reaction rate relates to experimental conditions and parameters.
Define reaction kinetics as the amount of reactant converted to product per unit time.
Relate reactant and product concentration changes to stoichiometric coefficients in the balanced equation.
Explain how concentrations, temperature, surface area, catalysts, and environmental conditions affect reaction rate.
Represent experimental observations with a consistent rate-law expression.
Use experiments to monitor reactant or product amounts and determine reaction rate.
Describe rate as proportional to each reactant concentration raised to a power.
Identify individual reaction orders and calculate overall order from the rate-law exponents.
Explain that the rate constant depends on temperature and has units determined by overall order.
Use comparisons of initial rates to determine reaction order for each reactant.
Determine a reaction’s rate law from concentration-versus-time data.
Infer reaction order from a graph of reactant concentration versus time.
Recognize first-order behavior when ln reactant concentration versus time is linear.
Recognize second-order behavior when reciprocal reactant concentration versus time is linear.
Use concentration-time slopes for zero-, first-, and second-order reactions to find the rate constant.
Relate constant first-order half-life to the rate constant using t₁/₂ = 0.693/k.
Identify radioactive decay as an example of first-order kinetics.
Write an elementary reaction’s rate law from its stoichiometry.
Infer an elementary reaction’s rate law from particles colliding in that step.
Recognize that simultaneous collisions involving three or more particles are uncommon.
Relate elementary reaction rate to collision frequency, energy, and particle orientation.
Explain that successful reactant collisions initiate bond breaking and bond formation.
Explain that effective collisions require sufficient energy and suitable orientation.
Use Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions to estimate how temperature changes the fraction of energetic collisions.
Represent activation energy and total energy change using an elementary reaction energy profile.
Identify the reaction coordinate as the axis describing progress through molecular rearrangement.
Interpret an energy profile from reactants through transition state to products and identify forward activation energy.
Recognize that elementary reactions break existing bonds and form new bonds.
Explain temperature dependence of elementary reaction rates using collision energies and the Arrhenius relationship.
Identify the components and structure of a reaction mechanism.
Describe a mechanism as sequential elementary steps involving reactants, intermediates, products, and catalysts.
Verify that combining elementary steps produces the overall balanced reaction.
Explain that an intermediate forms in one step and is consumed in another.
Use experimental detection of intermediates as evidence favoring one mechanism over another.
Determine a reaction’s rate law from a mechanism with an irreversible or rate-limiting first step.
Set the overall rate law from the molecularity of the slowest, rate-determining elementary step.
Determine a rate law when the mechanism’s first step is not rate limiting.
Apply approximations such as pre-equilibrium to derive a rate law when the first step is not limiting.
Represent activation energies and overall energy change for multistep reactions with an energy profile.
Construct a multistep energy profile using the energetics of each elementary reaction.
Explain how catalysts alter reaction mechanisms and affect reaction rate.
Explain that catalysts increase effective collisions or provide a pathway with lower activation energy.
Explain how catalysts can be consumed in one step and regenerated later while maintaining constant net concentration.
Describe catalysts that bind reactants, improve orientation, lower activation energy, and form bound intermediates.
Describe covalent or acid-base catalysis involving proton transfer and new intermediates.
Describe surface catalysis in which reactants or intermediates bind to a surface and form new steps.
Relate experimental observations to energy changes during chemical or physical transformations.
Recognize that temperature changes indicate energy changes in a system.
Classify energy changes as endothermic or exothermic during heating, cooling, phase changes, or chemical transformations.
Explain how exothermic and endothermic reactions transfer energy between the system and surroundings.
Explain why dissolving a substance can either release or absorb energy based on interaction strengths.
Represent a chemical or physical transformation using an energy diagram.
Use energy diagrams to show whether a physical or chemical process is endothermic or exothermic.
Relate thermal-energy transfer to collisions between molecules.
Explain that warmer bodies have particles with greater average kinetic energy.
Explain that particle collisions in thermal contact transfer energy as heat.
Describe thermal equilibrium as equal average kinetic energies and temperatures after heat transfer.
Calculate heat absorbed or released using substance amount, heat capacity, and temperature change.
Use q = mcΔT to quantify heat transfer and understand calorimetry measurements.
Apply conservation of energy to chemical and physical processes.
Explain why equal masses with different specific heats undergo different temperature changes for the same heat transfer.
Relate heating to increased system energy and cooling to decreased system energy.
Use specific heat and molar heat capacity in energy calculations.
Identify heating or cooling, phase transitions, and chemical reactions as major ways systems change energy.
Determine energy-flow direction during dissolution from the mixture’s temperature change.
Calculate phase-change heat using moles and molar enthalpy.
Explain energy changes during melting, boiling, freezing, and condensation, including constant temperature during phase change.
Relate energy absorbed in one phase change to energy released in its reverse process.
Calculate reaction heat from reacting moles and molar enthalpy.
Interpret reaction enthalpy as heat released or absorbed at constant pressure.
Explain heat transfer between products and surroundings as reactions reach thermal equilibrium.
Relate bond breaking and formation to chemical potential-energy differences and observed temperature changes.
Calculate reaction enthalpy from average energies of bonds broken and formed.
Explain that breaking and forming bonds changes the system’s potential energy.
Compare energy required to break reactant bonds with energy released forming product bonds to classify reaction energetics.
Calculate process enthalpy changes from standard enthalpies of formation.
Use formation-enthalpy tables to calculate standard reaction enthalpy.
Represent a chemical or physical process as a sequence of steps.
Break a process into individual steps, each with its own energy change.
Relate overall process enthalpy to the sum of enthalpy changes for individual steps.
Use energy conservation to explain why overall enthalpy equals the sum of step enthalpies.
Apply Hess’s law when reversing, scaling, or adding chemical equations and their enthalpy changes.
Relate reversible processes to the experimental observations that indicate equilibrium has been established.
Recognize that many physical and chemical processes, including proton transfer and electron transfer, are reversible.
Describe equilibrium as a state with no observable change, constant species concentrations or partial pressures, and reactants and products both present.
Explain that equilibrium is dynamic because forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates.
Use concentration, partial-pressure, or reaction-rate graphs to analyze how equilibrium is established.
Relate a reversible reaction’s direction to the relative rates of its forward and reverse reactions.
Predict net reactant-to-product or product-to-reactant conversion from the relative forward and reverse rates, including equilibrium when rates are equal.
Write Qc or Qp and corresponding K expressions for reversible reactions, recognizing that Q equals K at equilibrium.
Use concentration-based or partial-pressure-based mass-action expressions for reaction quotients and equilibrium constants.
Omit pure solids and liquids from reaction-quotient and equilibrium-constant expressions because their amounts do not affect the ratio.
Calculate Kc or Kp from measured equilibrium concentrations or partial pressures.
Determine an equilibrium constant using experimental equilibrium concentrations or partial pressures of reactants and products.
Relate the size of K to the relative equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products.
Interpret very large K values as near-complete reaction and very small values as minimal reaction.
Construct an overall equilibrium expression from the equilibrium expressions of constituent reactions.
Invert K when reversing a reaction.
Raise K to the corresponding power when all reaction coefficients are multiplied by a factor.
Multiply equilibrium constants when adding reactions to obtain an overall reaction.
Apply valid algebraic transformations of K expressions to reaction-quotient expressions.
Determine equilibrium concentrations or partial pressures from initial conditions, a balanced reaction, and K.
Predict equilibrium species concentrations or partial pressures using initial values, stoichiometry, and the appropriate equilibrium constant.
Use Q compared with K to predict reaction direction and identify dynamic equilibrium when Q equals K.
Model a reversible reaction system using particles.
Use particle diagrams to show reactant and product amounts before equilibrium and relate them to K.
Predict how an equilibrium system responds to an external stress using Le Châtelier’s principle.
Predict equilibrium responses to species addition or removal, temperature or pressure changes, volume changes, and dilution.
Predict how equilibrium stresses affect measurable properties such as pH, temperature, and solution color.

topics.title: 7.10 Reaction Quotient and Le Châtelier’s Principle

outcomes.text: Relate Q, K, and the direction a reversible reaction takes to reach a new equilibrium.
Explain that a disturbance changes Q relative to K and drives the system toward a state where they agree again.
Distinguish stresses that change only Q from temperature changes that alter K, with species redistributing accordingly.
Calculate salt solubility from its solubility-product constant, Ksp.
Relate salt dissolution as a reversible process whose extent is measured by Ksp.
Calculate solubility from Ksp and use it to compare the relative solubilities of substances.
Connect solubility rules quantitatively to Ksp, with Ksp values above one indicating soluble salts.
Calculate Ksp from the molar solubility of species in a saturated solution.
Determine salt solubility or Ksp effects from a common ion already present in solution.
Explain or calculate why adding a common ion decreases salt solubility using Le Châtelier’s principle or Ksp.
Calculate pH and pOH using Kw and concentrations of species in neutral water.
Relate hydronium and hydroxide concentrations to pH and pOH using logarithmic definitions.
Describe water autoionization using the equilibrium constant Kw.
Recognize that pure water is neutral, with equal pH and pOH and a pH of 7 at 25°C.
Explain how temperature-dependent Kw changes the pH of neutral pure water.

topics.title: 8.2 pH and pOH of Strong Acids and Bases

outcomes.text: Calculate pH and pOH from species concentrations in strong-acid and strong-base solutions.
Explain that strong acids completely ionize, making hydronium concentration equal to their initial concentration.
Explain that strong bases completely dissociate and determine hydroxide concentration from their stoichiometry.
Relate pH, pOH, and species concentrations in monoprotic weak-acid and weak-base solutions.
Explain that weak acids only partly ionize, leaving most acid molecules un-ionized.
Use Ka or pKa and initial concentration to describe and calculate weak-acid equilibrium and pH.
Explain that weak bases only partly ionize, so hydroxide concentration is below the initial base concentration.
Use Kb or pKb and initial concentration to describe and calculate weak-base equilibrium and pH.
Calculate weak-acid or weak-base percent ionization from equilibrium constants, initial concentrations, or equilibrium species.
Relate Ka and Kb for conjugate pairs through Kw, including their p-value relationship.
Relate major-species concentrations when weak and strong acids or bases are mixed.
Determine resulting pH after strong acid and strong base neutralization using the excess reagent.
Predict major species and pH when a weak acid reacts with a strong base, including buffer and equivalence cases.
Predict major species and pH when a weak base reacts with a strong acid, including buffer and equivalence cases.
Describe the equilibrium reached when a weak acid and weak base are mixed.
Relate buffer pH to pKa and the concentration ratio of conjugate base to conjugate acid using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.
Determine a buffer’s pH from its conjugate acid-base pair and their concentrations.
Explain mono- and polyprotic acid or base titration results using solution properties and components.
Interpret titration curves that show pH as titrant volume increases.
Use equivalence-point mole relationships to determine an analyte concentration.
Use half-equivalence-point concentrations and pH to determine a weak acid’s or base’s pKa or pKb.
Explain equivalence-point pH from the acid-base character of the species remaining in solution.
Use polyprotic titration curves to identify acidic protons, major species, and successive pKa values.

topics.title: 8.6 Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases

subtopics.title: 8.6 Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases

outcomes.text: Relate acid or base strength to the molecular or ionic structure.
Use electronegativity, inductive effects, resonance, and molecular structure to compare acid and base strengths.
Relate the predominant weak-acid or weak-base form to solution pH and pKa or pKb.
Predict whether protonated or deprotonated species predominates by comparing pH with pKa.
Explain how acid-base indicators change observable properties between protonated and deprotonated states.
Select an indicator whose pKa is near the equivalence-point pH for accurate titration results.
Relate buffer pH stability to reactions occurring when acid or base is added.
Explain how substantial amounts of both conjugate species let buffers consume added acid or base.
Relate buffer capacity to the relative concentrations of conjugate acid and conjugate base.
Explain that increasing both buffer component concentrations while preserving their ratio increases capacity without changing pH.
Predict whether a buffer better neutralizes added acid or base from the relative amounts of its conjugate pair.
Identify qualitatively how pH changes affect a salt’s solubility.
Recognize pH-sensitive salt solubility when an ion is a weak acid, weak base, or hydroxide, using Le Châtelier’s principle.
Identify the sign and relative size of entropy changes for chemical and physical processes.
Entropy generally rises when matter becomes more dispersed, including during phase changes, gas expansion, or increased gaseous product moles.
Entropy increases as energy becomes more dispersed, such as when rising temperature broadens gas particle kinetic-energy distributions.
Calculate standard entropy changes for chemical or physical processes using species’ standard molar entropies.
Find process entropy change by subtracting total reactant absolute entropies from total product absolute entropies.

topics.title: 9.3 Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability

outcomes.text: Determine whether a physical or chemical process is thermodynamically favored from its standard Gibbs free-energy change.
Recognize ΔG° as the Gibbs free-energy change when all substances are in their standard states.
Interpret a negative ΔG° as indicating a thermodynamically favored process.
Calculate standard Gibbs free-energy change from standard Gibbs free energies of formation.
Recognize that both enthalpy and entropy may determine whether a process is thermodynamically favored.
Calculate ΔG° from standard enthalpy change, standard entropy change, and temperature.
Predict favorable temperature ranges from the signs of ΔH° and ΔS°.
Explain kinetically why a thermodynamically favored reaction may proceed too slowly to measure.
Recognize that thermodynamically favored processes may be extremely slow or show no measurable progress.
Explain kinetic control as thermodynamic favorability constrained by a high activation energy, not necessarily equilibrium.
Use the relationships among K, ΔG°, and temperature to determine thermodynamic favorability.
Relate ΔG° less than zero to product-favored equilibrium and an equilibrium constant greater than one.
Use the exponential and logarithmic equations connecting K, ΔG°, R, and temperature.
Estimate how the equilibrium constant differs from one based on the size of ΔG° relative to RT.
Relate negative ΔG° to product-favored equilibrium and positive ΔG° to reactant-favored equilibrium.
Explain how salt solubility relates to enthalpy and entropy changes during dissolution.
Analyze dissolution free energy through lattice disruption, solvent reorganization, and solute–solvent interactions.
Explain how external energy or coupled reactions drive thermodynamically unfavorable processes.
Describe how electricity or light can supply energy for thermodynamically unfavorable processes.
Explain how coupling an unfavorable reaction with a favorable one can produce a desired product and negative overall ΔG°.
Relate electrochemical-cell components to the cell’s overall operation.
Explain how electrodes, half-cell solutions, salt bridges, and measuring devices determine cell behavior.
Distinguish galvanic cells, which use favored reactions, from electrolytic cells, which require energy for unfavored reactions.
Identify oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode in every electrochemical cell.
Determine cell favorability from standard cell potential and the cell’s half-reactions.
Relate positive voltage to thermodynamically favored redox reactions and negative voltage to reactions requiring external potential.
Calculate standard cell potential from oxidation and reduction half-reactions and their standard reduction potentials.
Use the relationship ΔG° = −nFE° to connect standard Gibbs free energy and cell potential.
Explain how departures from standard conditions affect an electrochemical cell’s potential.
Cell potential depends on active-species concentrations and becomes larger when the reaction is farther from equilibrium.
Le Châtelier’s principle does not apply to electrochemical systems because they are not at equilibrium.
Relate reaction quotient, equilibrium, and concentration changes to the magnitude and direction of cell potential.
Use qualitative Nernst-equation reasoning to determine how concentration changes affect cell potential.
Calculate charge transferred from changes in reactant and product amounts in an electrochemical cell.
Use Faraday’s laws to relate electron transfer, deposited mass, current, time, charge, and ionic charge.
